description: MATLAB's arithmetic, relational, logical, concatenation and bitwise operators together with the elementary elementwise math functions. Array (dot) operators act element by element while matrix operators follow linear-algebra rules, and since R2016b all binary elementwise operators expand compatible singleton dimensions implicitly.

tools.name: plus
tools.description: Elementwise addition, normally written with the + operator. Inputs must have compatible sizes: identical dimensions, or dimensions that are 1 and therefore expand implicitly. Use the functional form when you need to pass addition as a function handle, for example to `arrayfun` or `cellfun`.
tools.usage:
C = A + B
C = plus(A, B)

parameters.name: A, B
parameters.description: Arrays with compatible sizes, or one of them a scalar.

tools.notes: Implicit expansion (broadcasting) makes `repmat` unnecessary for most arithmetic. Adding two different integer classes is an error; convert one first.

tools.name: minus
tools.description: Elementwise subtraction, written with the - operator. Like addition it supports implicit expansion, which is the idiomatic way to centre data by subtracting a row of column means. The unary form `-A` negates every element.
tools.usage:
C = A - B
C = minus(A, B)
tools.notes: Subtracting unsigned integers saturates at 0 rather than wrapping: `uint8(3) - uint8(5)` is 0.

tools.name: times
tools.description: Elementwise multiplication, written with the .* operator, which multiplies corresponding elements of two arrays. This is the operator you want for scaling, windowing a signal, and applying a mask, as opposed to * which performs matrix multiplication. Implicit expansion lets a row or column vector scale a whole matrix.
tools.usage:
C = A .* B
C = times(A, B)
tools.notes: Forgetting the dot and writing * on two same-size matrices silently performs matrix multiplication when the inner dimensions agree, which is a classic source of wrong answers.

tools.name: mtimes
tools.description: Matrix multiplication, written with the * operator, following linear-algebra rules: the number of columns of A must equal the number of rows of B. Use it for linear transformations, systems of equations and inner or outer products. If either operand is a scalar it multiplies every element.
tools.usage:
C = A * B
C = mtimes(A, B)
tools.notes: Chain order matters for speed: for A*B*v with a vector v, MATLAB evaluates left to right, so writing A*(B*v) can be dramatically faster. `pagemtimes` multiplies stacks of matrices.

tools.name: rdivide
tools.description: Elementwise right division, written A ./ B, dividing each element of A by the corresponding element of B. It is the correct operator for normalizing data, computing ratios and converting units. Division by zero yields Inf or NaN rather than an error.
tools.usage:
C = A ./ B
C = rdivide(A, B)

parameters.name: B
parameters.description: Denominator array with a compatible size.

tools.example:
[10 20 30] ./ [2 5 10]
A = magic(3);
A ./ sum(A)          % normalize each column
1 ./ 0
tools.notes: `ldivide` (A .\ B) divides in the other direction. Integer elementwise division rounds; use `idivide` to choose the rounding rule explicitly.

tools.name: mrdivide
tools.description: Matrix right division, written x = B / A, which solves the system x*A = B. For square A it is equivalent to B*inv(A) but computed far more accurately and quickly via factorization. Its sibling `mldivide` (backslash) solves A*x = b and is the standard way to solve linear systems in MATLAB.
tools.usage:
x = B / A
x = mrdivide(B, A)

parameters.name: A
parameters.description: Coefficient matrix; may be square or rectangular.

tools.notes: B/A is mathematically (A'\B')'. Never write B*inv(A): it is slower and less accurate. For rank-deficient systems MATLAB returns a least-squares or basic solution and issues a warning.

tools.name: power
tools.description: Elementwise power, written A .^ B, raising each element of A to the corresponding element of B. Use it for polynomial evaluation on a grid, for squaring signals, and anywhere exponents vary element by element. Negative bases with fractional exponents produce complex results.
tools.usage:
C = A .^ B
C = power(A, B)

parameters.name: B
parameters.description: Exponent array with a compatible size.

tools.notes: `(-8).^(1/3)` returns a complex principal root; use `nthroot` for the real cube root. Squaring with `x.^2` is generally faster than `x.*x` only marginally, so choose for readability.

tools.name: mpower
tools.description: Matrix power, written A ^ n, which for a positive integer n repeatedly multiplies a square matrix by itself. For non-integer or matrix exponents it is computed through the eigendecomposition and may return complex results. Use it for Markov chain transition powers and repeated linear maps.
tools.usage:
C = A ^ B
C = mpower(A, B)

parameters.name: B
parameters.description: Scalar exponent (or square matrix when A is scalar).

tools.notes: For fractional powers of a matrix prefer the dedicated `sqrtm`, `logm` and `expm`, which are more accurate. A^n with large n can overflow; consider scaling or eigen-analysis.

tools.name: ctranspose
tools.description: Complex conjugate transpose, written A' , which flips a matrix over its diagonal and conjugates complex entries. The non-conjugate transpose `A.'` (`transpose`) only reorders elements. For real data the two are identical, which is why the difference is easy to overlook.
tools.usage:
B = A'
B = ctranspose(A)
B = A.'   % transpose, no conjugation
tools.notes: Use `.'` when transposing complex data you do not want conjugated, for example when reshaping FFT output. Inside a string, the apostrophe would be ambiguous, so use `transpose(A)` in generated code for clarity.

tools.name: horzcat
tools.description: Horizontal concatenation, normally written with square brackets and commas, joining arrays side by side along dimension 2. All inputs must have the same number of rows. Use the functional form to concatenate the contents of a cell array with `horzcat(C{:})`.
tools.usage:
C = [A, B]
C = horzcat(A1, ..., An)
tools.notes: Concatenating in a loop reallocates memory each time; preallocate or collect into a cell array and concatenate once. Concatenating a double with an int32 produces int32.

tools.name: vertcat
tools.description: Vertical concatenation, written with square brackets and semicolons, stacking arrays along dimension 1. Column counts must match across all inputs. It also concatenates tables, timetables and struct arrays with identical variables or fields.
tools.usage:
C = [A; B]
C = vertcat(A1, ..., An)
tools.notes: For tables the variable names and types must be compatible; use `outerjoin` or `[T1; T2(:, T1.Properties.VariableNames)]` when they differ in order.

tools.name: and
tools.description: Elementwise logical AND, written A & B, returning a logical array that is true where both inputs are nonzero. Use it to combine masks when filtering data. The short-circuit form && is for scalar conditions in if and while statements and stops evaluating as soon as the result is determined.
tools.usage:
C = A & B
C = and(A, B)
tf = expr1 && expr2   % short-circuit, scalars only

parameters.name: A, B
parameters.description: Logical or numeric arrays with compatible sizes.

tools.notes: Using & where && is needed still works for scalars but does not short-circuit, so a guard like `~isempty(x) & x(1)>0` errors on empty x. Prefer && in conditions.

tools.name: or
tools.description: Elementwise logical OR, written A | B, true where either input is nonzero. The short-circuit form || evaluates the second operand only if the first is false and requires scalar logical values. Use | for masks over arrays and || for control-flow conditions.
tools.usage:
C = A | B
C = or(A, B)
tf = expr1 || expr2   % short-circuit, scalars only

parameters.name: A, B
parameters.description: Logical or numeric arrays with compatible sizes.

tools.notes: Mixing | and & without parentheses is legal (& binds tighter) but easy to misread; parenthesize.

tools.name: not
tools.description: Elementwise logical NOT, written ~A, returning true where the input is zero and false elsewhere. Use it to invert masks and to negate predicate results such as `~isempty(x)` or `~ismember(a, b)`. The tilde is also used as a placeholder to ignore an output argument.
tools.usage:
C = ~A
C = not(A)
[~, idx] = max(v)   % ignore first output
tools.notes: Using ~ to skip an output is the idiomatic alternative to creating throwaway variables. In MATLAB ~= is the not-equal operator, not a negated assignment.

tools.name: xor
tools.description: Elementwise exclusive OR, true where exactly one of the two inputs is nonzero. Use it for parity checks, for detecting disagreement between two logical masks, and in simple cryptographic or error-detection code. There is no operator form; always call the function.
tools.usage: C = xor(A, B)

parameters.name: A, B
parameters.description: Logical or numeric arrays with compatible sizes.

tools.notes: For bit-level exclusive OR on integers use `bitxor` instead; `xor` treats any nonzero value as a single true.

tools.name: any
tools.description: Tests whether any element is nonzero or true, reducing along a dimension (columns by default) or over the whole array with the 'all' option. Use it to ask 'does at least one element satisfy this condition?' in guards and validation. NaN counts as true because it is nonzero.
tools.usage:
tf = any(A)
tf = any(A, dim)
tf = any(A, 'all')

parameters.name: 'all'
parameters.description: Reduce over every element, returning a scalar.

tools.example:
any([0 0 3])
A = [0 1; 0 0];
any(A)
any(A, 2)
any(A(:))
if any(isnan(data)), warning('NaNs present'), end
tools.notes: For a matrix, `any(A)` reduces columns and returns a row vector, so a scalar test needs `any(A(:))` or `any(A,'all')`.

tools.name: all
tools.description: Tests whether all elements are nonzero or true, reducing along a dimension or over the entire array with 'all'. Use it to validate that every element meets a condition before proceeding. An empty array returns true, which is the mathematically correct but occasionally surprising vacuous result.
tools.usage:
tf = all(A)
tf = all(A, dim)
tf = all(A, 'all')
tools.example:
all([1 2 3] > 0)
all([])
A = magic(4);
all(A > 0, 'all')
assert(all(isfinite(x)), 'x must be finite')
tools.notes: Because `all([])` is true, guard with `~isempty(x) && all(...)` when emptiness should fail the check.

tools.name: eq
tools.description: Elementwise equality comparison, written A == B, returning a logical array. The full family of relational operators is ==, ~=, <, <=, > and >= with functional names eq, ne, lt, le, gt and ge. They compare numeric, logical, char, string, datetime, duration and categorical values.
tools.usage:
tf = A == B
tf = eq(A, B)
tf = A ~= B
tf = A < B

parameters.name: A, B
parameters.description: Arrays with compatible sizes; one may be a scalar.

tools.example:
[1 2 3] == 2
"cat" == "cat"
abs(0.1 + 0.2 - 0.3) < 1e-12   % correct float comparison
0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3               % false
tools.notes: Never compare floating-point results with == ; compare the absolute difference against a tolerance, or use `ismembertol`. For whole-array equality including size and class, use `isequal`.

tools.name: isequal
tools.description: Returns a single logical value that is true when all inputs have the same size and the same contents, ignoring class differences among numeric types. It works recursively on cell arrays, structs, tables and objects, so it is the right tool for comparing whole data structures. `isequaln` is the variant that treats NaN values as equal.
tools.usage:
tf = isequal(A, B)
tf = isequal(A1, A2, ..., An)
tf = isequaln(A, B)

parameters.name: A1,...,An
parameters.description: Two or more values to compare.

tools.example:
isequal([1 2], [1 2])
isequal(int8(1), 1)
isequal(NaN, NaN)
isequaln(NaN, NaN)
isequal(struct('a',1), struct('a',1))
tools.notes: isequal returns false when sizes differ instead of erroring, which makes it safe for unit tests. It compares values, not handles, so two distinct handle objects with equal properties may still compare unequal.

tools.name: ismember
tools.description: Tests which elements of one array are members of another, returning a logical mask and optionally the index of the first match. Use it for set membership filtering, category lookups and validating an input against a list of allowed values. The 'rows' option matches whole rows.
tools.usage:
tf = ismember(A, B)
[tf, loc] = ismember(A, B)
tf = ismember(A, B, 'rows')

parameters.name: 'legacy'
parameters.description: Use pre-R2013a behaviour for index outputs.

tools.notes: Related set functions are `intersect`, `union`, `setdiff` and `setxor`. Use `ismembertol` for floating-point comparisons with a tolerance.

tools.name: bitand
tools.description: Computes the bitwise AND of two nonnegative integers or integer arrays. Use it to mask off bits when decoding packed status words, hardware registers or file headers. Both inputs must be of the same integer class, or doubles holding nonnegative integers.
tools.usage:
C = bitand(A, B)
C = bitand(A, B, assumedtype)

parameters.name: A, B
parameters.description: Nonnegative integer values or integer-class arrays.

parameters.name: assumedtype
parameters.description: Integer class to assume when inputs are doubles, for example 'uint32'.

tools.example:
bitand(uint8(12), uint8(10))
status = uint16(hex2dec('00F3'));
lowNibble = bitand(status, uint16(15))
dec2bin(bitand(uint8(12), uint8(10)), 8)
tools.notes: Bitwise functions require nonnegative inputs unless you pass an `assumedtype` for two's-complement handling. `bitcmp` complements all bits within a class.

tools.name: bitor
tools.description: Computes the bitwise OR of two integers or integer arrays, setting a bit in the result when it is set in either input. Use it to combine flag constants into a single options word before passing it to a driver or file format. Inputs must share an integer class or be nonnegative doubles.
tools.usage:
C = bitor(A, B)
C = bitor(A, B, assumedtype)

parameters.name: A, B
parameters.description: Nonnegative integer values or integer-class arrays.

parameters.name: assumedtype
parameters.description: Integer class to assume for double inputs.

tools.notes: To clear a flag, AND with the complement: `bitand(mode, bitcmp(FLAG_WRITE))`.

tools.name: bitxor
tools.description: Computes the bitwise exclusive OR, setting each result bit when exactly one input bit is set. Use it for toggling flags, computing simple checksums and parity, and lightweight scrambling. Applying the same XOR twice restores the original value.
tools.usage:
C = bitxor(A, B)
C = bitxor(A, B, assumedtype)

parameters.name: A, B
parameters.description: Nonnegative integer values or integer-class arrays.

parameters.name: assumedtype
parameters.description: Integer class to assume for double inputs.

tools.notes: This is a bit-level operation; use `xor` when you want a logical exclusive OR of truth values.

tools.name: bitshift
tools.description: Shifts the bits of an integer left (positive k) or right (negative k), which multiplies or divides by powers of two. Use it to pack and unpack fields inside a word, and to scale fixed-point values efficiently. Bits shifted past the class width are discarded.
tools.usage:
C = bitshift(A, k)
C = bitshift(A, k, assumedtype)

parameters.name: k
parameters.description: Number of positions; positive shifts left, negative shifts right.

parameters.name: assumedtype
parameters.description: Integer class to assume for double inputs.

tools.example:
bitshift(uint8(1), 3)
bitshift(uint8(160), -4)
word = uint16(0);
word = bitor(bitshift(uint16(5), 8), uint16(200))
tools.notes: Left shifts saturate at the class maximum rather than wrapping. Combine bitshift and bitand to extract a bit field: `bitand(bitshift(w,-8), uint16(255))`.

tools.name: abs
tools.description: Returns the absolute value of each element, or the complex modulus for complex input. Use it for magnitudes, error measurement against a tolerance, and the amplitude spectrum after an FFT. The output class matches the input class.
tools.usage: Y = abs(X)
tools.example:
abs([-3 0 4])
abs(3 + 4i)
err = abs(computed - expected);
max(err(:))
tools.notes: `abs(intmin('int8'))` saturates at 127 because 128 is not representable. For complex data `abs` gives the modulus and `angle` the phase.

tools.name: sign
tools.description: Returns -1, 0 or 1 according to the sign of each element, and for complex input returns the unit-modulus value x./abs(x). Use it to extract direction from a magnitude, to implement signum-based control laws, and to detect zero crossings via `diff(sign(x))`. The result of sign(0) is exactly 0.
tools.usage: Y = sign(X)
tools.notes: sign(NaN) is NaN. Because sign(0) is 0, zero-crossing detection with `diff(sign(x))` can report two transitions when a sample lands exactly on zero.

tools.name: sqrt
tools.description: Computes the elementwise square root, returning complex results for negative input rather than an error. Use it for magnitudes, RMS values, standard deviations from variances and geometric distances. For matrix square roots in the linear-algebra sense use `sqrtm`.
tools.usage: Y = sqrt(X)

parameters.name: X
parameters.description: Numeric array; negative values yield complex output.

tools.notes: Use `hypot(a,b)` instead of `sqrt(a.^2+b.^2)` to avoid intermediate overflow or underflow. `realsqrt` errors on negative input instead of returning complex values.

tools.name: exp
tools.description: Computes e raised to each element of the input. For complex input it follows Euler's formula, which makes it the basis of phasor and Fourier computations. Use it for exponential decay and growth models, softmax computations and probability densities.
tools.usage: Y = exp(X)
tools.notes: exp overflows to Inf above about 709 for doubles; subtract the maximum before exponentiating in softmax-style code. `expm1(x)` is accurate for tiny x where exp(x)-1 loses precision.

tools.name: log
tools.description: Computes the natural logarithm elementwise, returning complex values for negative input and -Inf for zero. Use it for log-likelihoods, decibel-free ratios, and to linearize exponential relationships before fitting. The related functions log10, log2 and log1p cover other bases and small-argument accuracy.
tools.usage: Y = log(X)

parameters.name: X
parameters.description: Numeric array; negative values yield complex output.

tools.example:
log(exp(2))
log(0)
log(-1)
log1p(1e-16)   % accurate where log(1+x) is not
tools.notes: For products of many small probabilities, sum logs instead of multiplying to avoid underflow. `reallog` errors rather than returning complex results for negative input.

tools.name: log10
tools.description: Computes the base-10 logarithm elementwise. It is the basis of decibel calculations (20*log10 for amplitude, 10*log10 for power) and of order-of-magnitude reasoning. Negative inputs return complex values.
tools.usage: Y = log10(X)
tools.notes: Guard against zeros before taking logs of spectra: `20*log10(max(abs(H), eps))` avoids -Inf.

tools.name: log2
tools.description: Computes the base-2 logarithm, and with two output arguments decomposes each value into a fraction and an exponent such that X = f .* 2.^e. Use it for information-theoretic entropy in bits, for sizing FFTs to powers of two, and for inspecting floating-point representations.
tools.usage:
Y = log2(X)
[F, E] = log2(X)
tools.notes: `nextpow2` and `pow2` are the usual companions for FFT sizing. The two-output form is exact and never loses precision.

tools.name: mod
tools.description: Returns the remainder after division with the sign of the divisor, which makes it the right choice for wrapping values into a range. Use it for circular indexing, angle wrapping, and periodic scheduling logic. mod(x,0) returns x.
tools.usage: b = mod(a, m)

parameters.name: m
parameters.description: Divisor array; result takes the sign of m.

tools.notes: mod and rem differ for negative operands: mod(-1,5) is 4 while rem(-1,5) is -1. For floating-point dividends the result is subject to rounding, so avoid exact equality tests on the remainder.

tools.name: rem
tools.description: Returns the remainder after division with the sign of the dividend, matching the behaviour of the C `%` operator and of truncated division. Use it when you want the remainder to keep the sign of the numerator, for example when splitting a signed duration into whole and fractional parts. rem(x,0) returns NaN.
tools.usage: r = rem(a, b)

parameters.name: b
parameters.description: Divisor array; result takes the sign of a.

tools.example:
rem(7, 3)
rem(-7, 3)
mod(-7, 3)
secondsPart = rem(totalSeconds, 60);
tools.notes: rem(a,b) equals a - b.*fix(a./b), whereas mod(a,b) equals a - b.*floor(a./b). Choose mod for wrapping and rem for truncation semantics.

tools.name: floor
tools.description: Rounds each element down toward negative infinity to the nearest integer. Use it for bin indices, for converting continuous positions to grid cells, and together with mod for integer division. The output remains the same class as the input, so floor of a double is still a double.
tools.usage: Y = floor(X)
tools.notes: floor, ceil, round and fix differ for negative values: floor(-2.7) is -3 while fix(-2.7) is -2. Convert to an integer class explicitly if you need an integer-typed result.

tools.name: ceil
tools.description: Rounds each element up toward positive infinity. Use it to compute the number of blocks needed to cover a quantity, to size buffers, and to find upper grid boundaries. It also works on duration and datetime values, rounding to a specified unit.
tools.usage:
Y = ceil(X)
Y = ceil(t, unit)
tools.notes: `ceil(a/b)` on integers can overflow for very large values; `idivide(a, b, 'ceil')` is safer for integer classes.

tools.name: round
tools.description: Rounds to the nearest value, with halves rounded away from zero, and optionally to a given number of decimal or significant digits. Use it for display-friendly values, for quantizing measurements, and for snapping to a resolution. It also rounds datetime and duration values to a named unit.
tools.usage:
Y = round(X)
Y = round(X, n)
Y = round(X, n, type)
Y = round(t, unit)

parameters.name: n
parameters.description: Number of digits; negative n rounds to tens, hundreds and so on.

tools.example:
round(2.5)
round(-2.5)
round(pi, 3)
round(12345, -2)
round(0.0012345, 2, 'significant')
tools.notes: MATLAB rounds halves away from zero, unlike Python's banker's rounding. Rounding a binary floating-point number to decimals is approximate: round(2.675, 2) yields 2.6800 but the stored value is not exactly 2.68.

tools.name: fix
tools.description: Rounds each element toward zero, discarding the fractional part regardless of sign. Use it for truncating division results and for splitting a value into integer and fractional components. It is the rounding rule used by C integer division and by `rem`.
tools.usage: Y = fix(X)
tools.notes: fix is the only one of the four rounding functions that is symmetric about zero. For integer-class arithmetic use `idivide(a,b,'fix')`.

tools.name: hypot
tools.description: Computes sqrt(a^2 + b^2) elementwise without intermediate overflow or underflow, which matters when the inputs are very large or very small. Use it for Euclidean distances, signal magnitudes from in-phase and quadrature components, and vector norms in two dimensions. It is more accurate than the naive expression for extreme values.
tools.usage: c = hypot(a, b)
tools.example:
hypot(3, 4)
hypot(1e200, 1e200)
sqrt(1e200^2 + 1e200^2)   % overflows to Inf
mag = hypot(I, Q);
tools.notes: For more than two components use `vecnorm(X, 2, dim)` or `norm` instead.

tools.name: nthroot
tools.description: Computes the real nth root of a value, returning a real negative result for negative input with an odd root. Use it when you need the real cube root or similar, which `.^(1/n)` does not give because it returns the complex principal root. Negative input with an even root is an error.
tools.usage: y = nthroot(X, n)

parameters.name: n
parameters.description: Real scalar or array of root orders; must be odd for negative X.

tools.notes: nthroot rejects complex input. For a geometric mean use `exp(mean(log(x)))` or `nthroot(prod(x), numel(x))` when the product does not overflow.

tools.name: gcd
tools.description: Computes the greatest common divisor elementwise, and with three outputs also returns the Bezout coefficients satisfying A.*C + B.*D = G. Use it for reducing fractions, finding common sampling periods and in modular arithmetic. Inputs must be integer-valued.
tools.usage:
G = gcd(A, B)
[G, C, D] = gcd(A, B)
tools.notes: gcd(0,0) is 0. Combine with `lcm` to find common periods of two rates: `lcm(p1, p2)`.
